sections.h2: Where is Baltimore, and why does it bill property tax differently from a county?
sections.html:
Baltimore sits in north-central Maryland on the Patapsco River, and it has been an independent city since 1851. It is almost entirely surrounded by Baltimore County but is politically separate from it, so there is no county tax bill layered on top of the city bill.

The city covers about 92 square miles, of which roughly 11 are water. Elevation runs from sea level at the harbor to around 480 feet in the northwest, which matters for older homes: lower blocks near the water see more flooding, while hillside neighborhoods deal more with drainage and old foundations.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. One city bill carries the city rate and the state rate together, and the same office that collects it also controls the annual tax sale. That makes a Baltimore tax balance a bigger deal than the same dollar amount in a county with a slower process.

sections.h2: What is the Baltimore property tax rate, and how is a bill calculated?
sections.html:
The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the State of Maryland adds $0.112 per $100, collected on the same bill and forwarded to the state. Together that is $2.360 per $100, or $2,360 a year on each $100,000 of taxable assessment before credits.

The City of Baltimore says the state Department of Assessments and Taxation sets each parcel's value and the city multiplies its own rate by that figure. The city rate is also listed on the budget office's tax-rate page, which shows $2.248 for fiscal 2027. A 2024 news report described it as the highest rate in the state.

ItemWhat the sources say
City real property rate$2.248 per $100 of assessed value
State rate on the city bill$0.112 per $100
Combined$2.360 per $100 (sum of the two rates)
Homestead credit cap, from July 1, 20264% a year on a principal residence
City transfer tax1.5% of the cash consideration
Recordation tax$5.00 per $500 of consideration paid

The transfer and recordation taxes have a reduced yield on sales over $1 million, and part of each goes to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Who pays them at closing is a contract term, so check your sales contract.

sections.h2: How did the 2026 reassessment affect Baltimore homes?
sections.html:
Baltimore was in Maryland's Group 2 reassessment, and residential full cash value rose 13.4% between January 1, 2023 and January 1, 2026. Statewide, Group 2 residential values rose 13.2%, so the city landed close to the state figure.

Notices went out on December 30, 2025. Increases are phased in evenly over three years, while decreases take effect in full in the 2026 tax year. Owners who live in the home and have applied for the homestead credit are protected by the 4% cap, which means a large jump in market value does not translate into a large jump in the taxable figure right away.

If you inherited a house or moved out years ago, check whether the credit is still attached. It requires a principal residence, so a house that has become a rental or sits empty can lose the cap and see the taxable value catch up faster.

sections.h2: When are Baltimore tax bills mailed, and what happens if they go unpaid?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed July 1 and are due on receipt, with a half-percent discount if paid by July 31. After October 1, unpaid tax accrues 1% interest plus a 1% monthly penalty.

Owner-occupied homes and small businesses with taxes under $100,000 can pay in two equal installments, with a small fee added to the second. A pending appeal does not excuse a late payment, but a successful appeal produces a refund with interest.

A property becomes eligible for the annual tax sale once it is behind by at least $750 on an owner-occupied residence or $250 on a non-owner-occupied one. The city sends a final bill and legal notice in the first week of February, a second letter in the first week of April, and holds the online sale in May.

  • First week of February: Final Bill and Legal Notice mailed to the address in land records.
  • First week of April: second letter.
  • May: the annual tax sale.
  • First week of July: post-sale informational letter.

Owners can stop a sale by redeeming, which means paying the winning bidder all claims, interest and costs. The city also runs a Tax Sale Deferral Program through Finance and Housing and Community Development that can keep a property out of the sale for a year.

sections.h2: What other city charges can become a lien on a Baltimore house?
sections.html:
Unpaid annual registration fees for non-owner-occupied property are a lien and are subject to tax sale, according to the Department of Housing and Community Development. That catches many sellers by surprise, because the fees are small each year and easy to miss on a rental or a vacant house you inherited.

The housing department's information sheet lists the fee structure in effect at the time it was published:

  • 1- and 2-family dwellings: $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Multifamily dwellings: $35 per dwelling unit or $25 per rooming unit.
  • Vacant residential structures: $100 per structure plus $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Vacant lots: $25 per lot.

Owners of registered vacant buildings must keep them clean and secure until they are razed or rehabilitated, and the city bills the owner if it does the work first. As of mid-2024 the housing department reported 13,411 vacant building notices, 863 of them on city-owned property.

State law passed in 2024 also lets the City Council set a special tax rate on abandoned properties, effective June 1, 2024. The news report we read said no rate had been set at that time, so confirm with the city before assuming one applies to your property.

sections.h2: What is the economy and housing stock behind a Baltimore sale?
sections.html:
Johns Hopkins University and Johns Hopkins Hospital are the largest employers, and the city's gross domestic product was reported at about $62 billion in 2023. Other named employers include Under Armour, McCormick and T. Rowe Price. The port is another anchor, with a 2014 figure of 14,630 direct jobs.

Housing is dominated by rowhouses, many with brick or formstone fronts. The city has more than 65,000 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, which is more than any other American city. Historic status can affect what exterior work you are allowed to do, so ask before you assume a quick cosmetic fix is permitted.

Population was 585,708 in the 2020 census and an estimated 569,997 for 2025, down from a peak of 949,708 in 1950. Neighborhoods named in the source include Canton, Fells Point, Federal Hill, Highlandtown, Roland Park and Pimlico, each with its own mix of owners and renters.

sections.h2: How do roads, rail and weather affect a Baltimore house?
sections.html:
Baltimore has a humid subtropical climate, with a July average near 80.7 degrees Fahrenheit and a January average near 35.8. Annual precipitation is about 45 inches at BWI and seasonal snowfall averages about 19 inches.

Hurricanes or their remnants can flood parts of downtown even though the city is not in a typical storm-surge zone. Buyers and inspectors look hard at basements, rear additions and roofs on rowhouses after a wet year.

Getting around is easier than in most Maryland places. Penn Station is among the nation's busiest rail stations, MARC runs three lines to Washington, Light RailLink runs from Hunt Valley to BWI, and Metro SubwayLink runs from downtown to Owings Mills. I-95 passes through the Fort McHenry Tunnel and I-83 is the Jones Falls Expressway. The Francis Scott Key Bridge on I-695 collapsed in March 2024.

sections.h2: What should a Baltimore seller with tax due do first?
sections.html:
Start by finding out what you owe and whether the property has been marked for the May sale. The collections call center is at 410-396-3000, and assessment questions and credits go to the state office at 410-767-8250.

  1. Pull the current bill on the city payment site and note any balance carried from earlier years.
  2. Check whether registration or other city charges are attached to the account.
  3. Ask for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date.
  4. Tell the title company early so the payoff is built into the settlement statement.

If money is tight, a payment plan or the deferral program may buy time. If the house needs work and the balance keeps growing, selling as-is for cash can be a cleaner way to clear the lien from the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state adds $0.112 per $100 on the same bill. That is $2.360 combined, before any credits.

faqs.q: Does Baltimore property tax go up when my house is reassessed?
faqs.a: Not all at once for most owners. Increases are phased in over three years, and a principal residence with the homestead credit is capped at 4% a year from July 1, 2026. Baltimore's residential values rose 13.4% in the 2026 reassessment.

faqs.q: How much unpaid tax puts a Baltimore house into the tax sale?
faqs.a: The city says a property becomes eligible once it is delinquent by at least $750 for an owner-occupied residence or $250 for other property. The sale is held online each May after notices in February and April.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Baltimore house that is already in the tax sale process?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but timing matters. The city says owners can stop a sale by redeeming, so ask the collections office for a payoff figure and tell your title company right away.

faqs.q: Do unpaid rental registration fees affect a sale?
faqs.a: They can. The housing department states that unpaid registration fees are a lien against the property and subject to tax sale, so clear them before closing.

faqs.q: What are the Baltimore transfer and recordation taxes?
faqs.a: The city lists a transfer tax of 1.5% of the cash consideration and a recordation tax of $5.00 per $500 of consideration. Who pays each is negotiated in the contract.
